CHAPTER 8.1 · LEARNING AREA 8

CHAPTER 8.1 · LEARNING AREA 8 · JANUARY

Scalar product, vector product and Hesse normal form

Two ways of multiplying vectors, and both have a clear meaning: the scalar product measures how much two directions agree, and so it gives you every angle. The vector product builds a vector that is perpendicular to both, and its length is an area. With this normal vector you describe planes briefly and elegantly in normal and coordinate form.

10 LESSONS3 UNITS4 WIDGETS1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • calculate the scalar product and use it to find angles, orthogonality and projections
  • calculate the vector product and interpret it as a perpendicular vector and as an area
  • find the normal vector of a plane and set up the normal and coordinate form
  • calculate trace points and describe the position of a plane in the coordinate system
  • set up the Hesse normal form for lines in the plane and for planes and interpret it as a distance with a sign

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Scalar product and vector product

If you pull a sledge with the force $\vec F$ along the path $\vec s$, only the part of the force in the direction of the path does work: $W = |\vec F| \cdot |\vec s| \cdot \cos\varphi$. Surprisingly, the simple calculation $F_1 s_1 + F_2 s_2 + F_3 s_3$ gives the same. This sum is called the scalar product, and its result is a number.

Because $\vec a \circ \vec b = |\vec a| \cdot |\vec b| \cdot \cos\varphi$, the scalar product gives you the angle between two vectors. If it is $0$, they are perpendicular. Dividing by $|\vec a|$ gives the length of the projection of $\vec b$ onto the direction of $\vec a$.

The vector product $\vec a \times \vec b$, on the other hand, is a vector. It is perpendicular to $\vec a$ and to $\vec b$, and its length is the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\vec a$ and $\vec b$. Swapping the factors reverses its direction. Parallel vectors have the vector product $\vec 0$.

KEY POINT · SCALAR PRODUCT AND VECTOR PRODUCT

Scalar product: $\vec a \circ \vec b = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3 = |\vec a| \cdot |\vec b| \cdot \cos\varphi$, so $\cos\varphi = \dfrac{\vec a \circ \vec b}{|\vec a| \cdot |\vec b|}$

Vector product: $\vec a \times \vec b = \begin{pmatrix} a_2 b_3 - a_3 b_2 \\ a_3 b_1 - a_1 b_3 \\ a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1 \end{pmatrix}$ is perpendicular to $\vec a$ and $\vec b$

$|\vec a \times \vec b| = |\vec a| \cdot |\vec b| \cdot \sin\varphi$ = area of the parallelogram; the triangle has half of it.

Notation: In this book $\vec a \circ \vec b$ stands for the scalar product. Many books and the online training write $\vec a \cdot \vec b$; it means the same.

Memory aid for the vector product: The first row uses components 2 and 3, the second 3 and 1, the third 1 and 2, always “crosswise”. Check: the result times $\vec a$ must give $0$.

EXAMPLE 1 · ANGLE AND PROJECTION

Calculate the angle between $\vec a = (1, 2, 2)$ and $\vec b = (2, -1, 2)$ and the length of the projection of $\vec b$ onto $\vec a$.

$\vec a \circ \vec b = 2 - 2 + 4 = 4$, $|\vec a| = |\vec b| = 3$: $\cos\varphi = \tfrac49$, $\varphi \approx 63.6^\circ$.

Projection: $\dfrac{\vec a \circ \vec b}{|\vec a|} = \tfrac43$

EXAMPLE 2 · TRIANGLE IN SPACE

Calculate the area of the triangle $A(1, 0, 0)$, $B(0, 2, 0)$, $C(0, 0, 3)$.

$\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} = (-1, 2, 0) \times (-1, 0, 3) = (6, 3, 2)$, length $\sqrt{36 + 9 + 4} = 7$.

$A = \tfrac72 = 3.5$. Check: $(6, 3, 2) \circ (-1, 2, 0) = 0$ ✔

EXERCISES

a) Calculate $(3, -1, 2) \circ (1, 4, 0)$.   b) What angle do $(1, 0, 0)$ and $(1, 1, 0)$ enclose?   c) $|\vec a| = 3$, $|\vec b| = 4$, $\varphi = 60^\circ$. Calculate $\vec a \circ \vec b$.

a) $3 - 4 + 0 = -1$, the angle is obtuse   b) $\cos\varphi = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, $45^\circ$   c) $3 \cdot 4 \cdot \tfrac12 = 6$

Calculate $(1, 2, 3) \times (4, 5, 6)$ and check that the result is perpendicular to both factors.

$(-3, 6, -3)$. $(-3, 6, -3) \circ (1, 2, 3) = -3 + 12 - 9 = 0$ ✔, $\circ\,(4, 5, 6) = -12 + 30 - 18 = 0$ ✔

The parallelogram $ABCD$ has $A(1, 0, 2)$, $B(3, 1, 2)$ and $D(1, 2, 4)$. Find $C$ and the area.

$\vec{OC} = \vec{OB} + \vec{AD}$: $C(3, 3, 4)$. $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AD} = (2, 1, 0) \times (0, 2, 2) = (2, -4, 4)$, length $6$.

A force $\vec F = (10, 0, 5)$ N moves a body by $\vec s = (4, 3, 0)$ m. Calculate the work $W = \vec F \circ \vec s$ and the angle between force and path.

$W = 40$ J. $|\vec F| = \sqrt{125} \approx 11.18$, $|\vec s| = 5$: $\cos\varphi \approx 0.716$, $\varphi \approx 44.3^\circ$.

Show for $\vec a = (1, 2, 2)$ and $\vec b = (2, -1, 2)$: $|\vec a \times \vec b|^2 + (\vec a \circ \vec b)^2 = |\vec a|^2 \cdot |\vec b|^2$. Justify the formula in general with $\sin^2\varphi + \cos^2\varphi = 1$.

$\vec a \times \vec b = (6, 2, -5)$, squared $65$; $(\vec a \circ \vec b)^2 = 16$; $65 + 16 = 81 = 9 \cdot 9$ ✔ In general: $|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2 \sin^2\varphi + |\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2 \cos^2\varphi = |\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2$.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Orthogonality, normal vector and coordinate form

A plane is fixed by a point $P$ and a direction $\vec n$ perpendicular to it, just as a table top is fixed by a point and the table leg. A point $X$ lies in the plane exactly when the connecting vector $\vec{PX}$ is perpendicular to $\vec n$: $(\vec x - \vec p) \circ \vec n = 0$.

Multiplying out the normal form gives the coordinate form $ax + by + cz = d$. Its coefficients form a normal vector $(a, b, c)$, and the right-hand side is $d = \vec n \circ \vec p$. If you know three points, the vector product of two direction vectors gives the normal vector. The trace points are the points of intersection with the axes: set two coordinates to zero and work out the third.

KEY POINT · NORMAL AND COORDINATE FORM

Orthogonality condition: $\vec a \perp \vec b \iff \vec a \circ \vec b = 0$ (for $\vec a, \vec b \neq \vec 0$)

Normal form: $E\colon (\vec x - \vec p) \circ \vec n = 0$ · Coordinate form: $E\colon n_1 x + n_2 y + n_3 z = d$ with $d = \vec n \circ \vec p$

Normal vector from the parametric form: $\vec n = \vec u \times \vec v$ for the direction vectors $\vec u$, $\vec v$

Intercept form: If $E$ has the trace points $(a, 0, 0)$, $(0, b, 0)$, $(0, 0, c)$, then $\tfrac xa + \tfrac yb + \tfrac zc = 1$.

Relative position of planes: If the normal vectors are multiples of each other, the planes are parallel or identical. If their scalar product is $0$, the planes are perpendicular.

INTERACTIVE · FROM PARAMETRIC FORM TO COORDINATE FORM

Enter the position vector and the direction vectors: the widget forms the normal vector with the vector product, sets up the coordinate equation and draws the trace triangle.

EXAMPLE 3 · THROUGH THREE POINTS

Set up a coordinate equation of the plane through $A(1, 1, 0)$, $B(3, 1, 1)$, $C(1, 4, 2)$ and find its trace points.

$\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} = (2, 0, 1) \times (0, 3, 2) = (-3, -4, 6)$, times $-1$: $\vec n = (3, 4, -6)$, $d = \vec n \circ \vec a = 7$.

$3x + 4y - 6z = 7$, trace points $(\tfrac73, 0, 0)$, $(0, \tfrac74, 0)$, $(0, 0, -\tfrac76)$

EXAMPLE 4 · FROM THE NORMAL FORM

Convert $E\colon \left(\vec x - (2, -1, 3)\right) \circ (1, 2, -2) = 0$ into the coordinate form.

$d = (1, 2, -2) \circ (2, -1, 3) = 2 - 2 - 6 = -6$.

$x + 2y - 2z = -6$. Check with $P$: $2 - 2 - 6 = -6$ ✔

EXERCISES

Give a normal vector of $E\colon 2x - y + 3z = 5$. Is $(4, -2, 6)$ one as well? And $(2, 1, 3)$?

$(2, -1, 3)$; $(4, -2, 6)$ yes (a multiple), $(2, 1, 3)$ no.

Set up the coordinate equation of the plane through $A(1, 2, 0)$ with the normal vector $(2, 1, -1)$.

$d = 2 + 2 + 0 = 4$: $2x + y - z = 4$

Find the trace points of $2x + 3y + 6z = 12$, sketch the trace triangle and calculate its area with the vector product.

$(6, 0, 0)$, $(0, 4, 0)$, $(0, 0, 2)$. $(-6, 4, 0) \times (-6, 0, 2) = (8, 12, 24)$, length $28$: area $14$.

For which $t$ is $(t, 2, 1)$ perpendicular to $(3, -1, 4)$?

$3t - 2 + 4 = 0$: $t = -\tfrac23$

Find the plane through $A(1, 0, 0)$, $B(0, 2, 0)$, $C(0, 0, 3)$ in coordinate form. Show that it can also be written as $\tfrac x1 + \tfrac y2 + \tfrac z3 = 1$.

With Example 2: $\vec n = (6, 3, 2)$, $d = 6$: $6x + 3y + 2z = 6$. Dividing by $6$: $x + \tfrac y2 + \tfrac z3 = 1$; the denominators are the intercepts on the axes.

UNIT 32 LESSONS

3The Hesse normal form

The line $g\colon 3x + 4y = 10$ in the plane has the normal vector $(3, 4)$ of length $5$. If you divide the equation by $5$, it becomes a unit vector: $0.6x + 0.8y - 2 = 0$. If you now substitute a point, you get its distance: for $O$ the value $-2$, for $P(4, 3)$ the value $2.4 + 2.4 - 2 = 2.8$.

Why? The expression $(\vec x - \vec p) \circ \vec n_0$ is the length of the projection of $\vec{PX}$ onto the normal direction, and that is exactly the distance from $X$ to the line or plane, with a sign. This equation with a normal vector of length $1$ is called the Hesse normal form, after Otto Hesse. The sign is usually chosen so that the constant $d \ge 0$; then $\vec n_0$ points away from the origin, and $d$ is the distance of the origin.

KEY POINT · HESSE NORMAL FORM

$(\vec x - \vec p) \circ \vec n_0 = 0$ with $|\vec n_0| = 1$. From the coordinate form: $\dfrac{n_1 x + n_2 y + n_3 z - d}{\sqrt{n_1^2 + n_2^2 + n_3^2}} = 0$, in the plane without $z$.

Substituting a point $Q$ gives its distance with a sign. Same sign: same side. With $d \ge 0$, negative means: on the side of the origin.

Otto Hesse (1811–1874) taught in Königsberg, Heidelberg and Munich. The normal form appears in his widely used textbooks, for example the Vorlesungen über analytische Geometrie des Raumes (Leipzig 1861). Source: MacTutor, “Otto Hesse”.

Outlook: In Chapter 8.3 the Hesse normal form gives all distances to planes, including that of skew lines.

INTERACTIVE · HESSE NORMAL FORM OF A LINE

Drag the base point $A$ and the point $P$ and rotate the normal vector. The value of the left-hand side is the distance from $P$ to the line, with a sign.

EXAMPLE 5 · LINE IN THE PLANE

Give the Hesse normal form of $g\colon y = 2x + 1$ and find the distance from $P(3, 2)$.

$-2x + y = 1$ (right-hand side $\ge 0$), $|\vec n| = \sqrt5$: $\dfrac{-2x + y - 1}{\sqrt5} = 0$.

Substitute $P$: $\tfrac{-6 + 2 - 1}{\sqrt5} = -\sqrt5$. $d(P, g) = \sqrt5 \approx 2.24$, on the side of the origin.

EXAMPLE 6 · PLANE IN SPACE

$E\colon 2x - y + 2z = -9$. Find the Hesse normal form, the distance of the origin and the distance of $Q(1, 2, 3)$.

Multiply by $-1$ so that $d \ge 0$: $-2x + y - 2z = 9$, $|\vec n| = 3$, HNF $\tfrac13(-2x + y - 2z - 9) = 0$. Origin: distance $3$.

$Q$: $\tfrac13(-2 + 2 - 6 - 9) = -5$: $d(Q, E) = 5$, on the same side as the origin.

EXERCISES

Give the Hesse normal form of $E\colon 2x + 2y - z = 6$. How far are the origin and $P(4, 4, 1)$ from $E$?

$\tfrac13(2x + 2y - z - 6) = 0$. Origin: $2$. $P$: $\tfrac13(8 + 8 - 1 - 6) = 3$, on the other side from the origin.

Calculate the distance of the point $P(5, 5)$ from the line $g\colon 3x + 4y = 10$.

$\tfrac{15 + 20 - 10}{5} = 5$

Find the two planes that are parallel to $E\colon 2x + y + 2z = 6$ and at distance $2$ from it.

Same normal vector, $|\vec n| = 3$: $\tfrac{|d - 6|}{3} = 2$, so $d = 12$ or $d = 0$: $2x + y + 2z = 12$ and $2x + y + 2z = 0$.

Find the set of all points that are equally far from $E_1\colon x + 2y + 2z = 3$ and $E_2\colon 2x - y + 2z = 6$.

Set the Hesse normal forms equal in absolute value: $\tfrac{x + 2y + 2z - 3}{3} = \pm \tfrac{2x - y + 2z - 6}{3}$.

With $+$: $-x + 3y + 3 = 0$, i.e. $x - 3y = 3$. With $-$: $3x + y + 4z = 9$. Two planes that bisect the angles between $E_1$ and $E_2$. They are perpendicular to each other: $(1, -3, 0) \circ (3, 1, 4) = 0$.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Is the triangle $A(0, 0, 0)$, $B(2, 0, 0)$, $C(1, 1, \sqrt2)$ equilateral? Also calculate the angle at $A$.

All sides have length $2$: yes. $\cos\alpha = \tfrac{\vec{AB} \circ \vec{AC}}{4} = \tfrac24$, $\alpha = 60^\circ$ ✔

Connecting with Year 11: How does $g\colon \vec x = (1, 0, 0) + t(1, 1, 0)$ lie relative to $E\colon x - y + z = 1$? Use the scalar product of the direction vector and the normal vector.

$(1, 1, 0) \circ (1, -1, 1) = 0$: $g$ is parallel to $E$ or lies in it. Point test with $(1, 0, 0)$: $1 = 1$ ✔, so $g$ lies in $E$.

What angle does the space diagonal of a cube make with an edge that starts at the same corner?

$(1, 1, 1)$ and $(1, 0, 0)$: $\cos\varphi = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, $\varphi \approx 54.7^\circ$.

Prove with the scalar product: the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular to each other.

The rhombus is spanned by $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ with $|\vec a| = |\vec b|$; its diagonals are $\vec a + \vec b$ and $\vec a - \vec b$.

$(\vec a + \vec b) \circ (\vec a - \vec b) = \vec a \circ \vec a - \vec b \circ \vec b = |\vec a|^2 - |\vec b|^2 = 0$.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

A formula in stone

The Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton (1805–1865) searched for years for a way to calculate with points in space just as with complex numbers in the plane. On Monday, 16 October 1843, he was walking with his wife along the Royal Canal in Dublin to a meeting of the Royal Irish Academy. Then the solution came to him. He carved it into the stone of Broome Bridge: $i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1$.

Hamilton called the new numbers quaternions. If you multiply two quaternions that consist only of the parts with $i$, $j$ and $k$, the result contains both things you have learnt in this chapter: the number part is the negative scalar product, and the rest is the vector product of the two vectors. Today quaternions control rotations in computer games and in space travel.

Source: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: biography “William Rowan Hamilton”.
